newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: HOWARD SAYS GOVERNMENT TO REEXAMINE MEDIA OWNERSHIP LAWS
The Prime Minister says the Federal Government will soon re-examine Australia's media cross-ownership laws.

John Howard was responding to a question about the ownership of Fairfax newspapers at an awards dinner for journalists in Melbourne. Mr Howard says he's always been skeptical about current cross-ownership prohibitions claiming he's never been a fan of the rules which limit a company's ability to have holdings in various parts of the media .
ANU OFFICIAL SAYS CONFIDENCE PROPER PROCESSES APPLIED
The Vice-Chancellor of the Australian National University says he's not aware any member of the Council has tried to influence the outcome of an academic assessment.
Independent Senator, Mal Colston, has denied claims he tried to use his position on a university board to help the academic progress of his son who was studying there.

Professor Deane Terrell says because of undertakings the University makes to students and the requirements of privacy legislation, the University won't comment on circumstances relating to an individual student's enrolment.
Professor Terrell says he's confident the University's processes for the review of academic process have been properly applied.
OPPOSITION SAYS SORRY ISN'T GOOD ENOUGH
The Federal Opposition says the Government's first year in office has been marked by a string of broken promises and a decline in job security.
Prime Minister John Howard will mark the anniversary, this weekend, with a keynote address to the New South Wales Liberal Council in Sydney.

Opposition leader, Kim Beazley, says before the election, Mr Howard said no promises to individuals would be broken. But he says in Government the stratgey used to deal with broken promises has been to apologise, which he says isn't good enough. The Prime Minister's office says the Government has kept faith with families, small busines, the environment movement and battlers, while the main election promises have been kept.
AMA URGING PEOPLE TO DROP PRIVATE HEALTH INSURANCE
The Federal Government's productivity Commission will report today on ways to prevent the dramatic slide in private health insurance membership.

But greeting the report is a call from the Australian Medical Association for people to drop private health cover. AMA vice-president David Brand says less than five per cent of the community really need private cover.
Doctor Brand says people would be better off paying for their private medical expenses out of their own pockets.
LAST DAY FOR TENDERS ON BRYANT'S HOUSE
Buyers have their last chance today to bid for the Hobart home of mass murderer Martin Bryant.
The house in New Town, Hobart, has been valued at A$211,000. Tenders close at noon. The proceeds of the sale will go to victims of the Port Arthur shootings and their families.
SABOTAGE ATTEMPT ON MELBOURNE'S GRAND PRIX TRACK
In Melbourne, organisers of the Australian Grand Prix say it's too early to tell if the race's starting time will be affected by what appears to be a deliberate attempt to sabotage the race.

An oil slick about half-a-kilometre long was found in front of the pits overnight. Fire Brigade Inspector, Bruce Barrett, says the track's being cleaned, but there's little doubt it was a deliberate act. Preliminary track events are due to start on Thursday.
The Save Albert Park group which has protested strongly against the race venue is disassociating itself from the spill.
MAN ARRESTED OVER BANK HOLD-UP

Police have arrested a man over yesterday's armed hold-up at a bank in Sydney's north. Three men, armed with a knife and baton, threatened staff and customers at the ANZ's Forestville branch before escaping with an undisclosed sum of money.
SENATE HEARING INTO CLOSURE OF ABC INTERNATIONAL SERVICES
Communications Minister Richard Alston has told a Senate hearing that ABC reviewer Bob Mansfield made a pretty strong case for the termination of the ABC's international services.

The Mansfield report said the ABC should cease broadcasting Radio Australia and close Australia Television if it can't be sold. A Senate inquiry into the proposed closures will report a week before the Budget, but the Minister's told a Senate hearing the decision will have been made in pre-budget deliberations.
Senator Alston has also ruled out further cuts to the ABC and endorsed the leadership of ABC managing director Brian Johns.
BURKE TRIAL DECISION TODAY
Former West Australian Premier Brian Burke will be told today whether he has been found guilty or not guilty of stealing from the Labor Party.

Mr Burke, who turned 50 on Tuesday, is accused of stealing between A$70,0000 and A$122,000 in campaign donations while he was Premier in the 1980s. It's alleged he used the money to buy stamps for his personal collection. Mr Burke has denied any wrongdoing.
PERTH ARMED HOLD-UP

Police are investigating an armed hold-up at a deli in Beechboro, in Perth's north-east. A man threatened staff at the Timberland Deli on Beechboro Road with a knife before fleeing in a white Holden Commodore driven by another man.
UN ENVOY TOLD ABORIGINES WANT CEREMONIES TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT
An Aboriginal council in Alice Springs has told a United Nations envoy they want enterprise agreement style awards developed to help Aborigines find employment in mainstream businesses.
Representatives of Tangentyere council told the U.N. Special Rapporteur on Religious Intolerance that cultural obligations can interfere with an Aborigine's ability to gain employment.

The Council's Mike Bowden says there are already award opportunities in some Aboriginal organisations which take into account of cultural obligations. He says it should be made possible for employers to accommodate the time an Aboriginal person may need to take off work.
HOWARD SAYS HE'S A "COMMON-LAW MAN"

The Prime Minister, John Howard, says he believes Australia's common law approach is superior to having a Bill of Rights. Mr Howard told a media dinner in Melbourne last night that he was a "common-law man".

His comments follow recents remarks signalling he'll reject the States' attempts to change the way the High Court operates. Mr Howard says the track record of countries with a Bill of Rights is no better than countries that have a common law approach. He says Bills of Rights have a tendency to leave things out or over-prescribe.
NRMA TO MAKE DONATION TO FLOOD AFFECTED
The Board of the NRMA has voted to make a A$200,000 donation to some of the people affected by floods in the New South Wales north over the past six months.
The offer follows a motion from director Richard Talbot for the Board to make a A$1 million ex-gratia payment to Coffs Harbour residents who recently had storm claims rejected.
The company believed damage to properties during a violent storm event in late November was caused by flood not rain water, and about 70 claims were rejected.
The A$200,000 donation will be distributed by a yet unnamed charity.
